scenes.name: lower precision pays off twice
scenes.visual: A dual-arrow diagram showing the double benefit of quantization. One arrow points to tensor cores: fewer bits means more operations per cycle. The other arrow points to the memory bus: fewer bytes per weight cuts memory traffic across the bus.

beats.say: Lower precision is the single lever that attacks both bottlenecks at the exact same time.
beats.show: A central number chip labeled 'Fewer bits per number' illuminates in gold.

beats.say: On the arithmetic side, narrower numbers allow tensor cores to process twice as many calculations each second.
beats.show: An amber arrow extends upward to the tensor core: 'More operations through tensor cores'.

beats.say: On the memory side, narrower numbers mean fewer bytes cross the bus for every weight. You move less data to do the same work.
beats.show: A coral arrow extends downward to the bus: 'Fewer bytes across the memory bus'. Takeaway: 'lower precision accelerates arithmetic while cutting memory traffic in half'.

scenes.name: binary long multiplication and the square law
scenes.visual: A worked binary long multiplication: 11 (1011) multiplied by 13 (1101) = 143 (10001111). A 4x4 grid of AND gates demonstrates that multiplier circuit area scales with the square of the bit width.

beats.say: Multiplying in binary is simply long multiplication with a trivial times table: each digit is either zero or one.
beats.show: Binary multiplication sets up: '1011 (11)' on top, '1101 (13)' below, with an arithmetic line beneath.

beats.say: Multiply eleven by thirteen, and the shifted rows sum to one hundred and forty-three.
beats.show: The four shifted partial products appear and sum: '10001111 = 128 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 143'.

beats.say: Every bit of the first number pairs with every bit of the second through an A N D gate. The work grows with the square of the width.
beats.show: A 4 by 4 grid of 16 AND gates illuminates: 'width × width = 4 × 4 = 16 gates'.

beats.say: Sixteen gates at four bits, sixty-four at eight bits, two hundred and fifty-six at sixteen bits, and over a thousand at thirty-two bits. Halve the bit width, and the multiplier circuit shrinks to a quarter.
beats.show: Four multiplier area blocks scale up: 16 gates (4-bit), 64 gates (8-bit), 256 gates (16-bit), and 1,024 gates (32-bit). Takeaway: 'multiplier area scales with width squared: narrow numbers shrink circuits by 4×'.

scenes.name: why tensor cores double instead of quadruple
scenes.visual: A physical area allocation diagram. The silicon footprint of one 32-bit multiplier can physically fit sixteen 8-bit multipliers. Yet the tensor core throughput doubles rather than quadrupling, showing the operand delivery bottleneck.

beats.say: By silicon area alone, the footprint of one thirty-two-bit multiplier can fit sixteen eight-bit multipliers.
beats.show: A large 32-bit square (1,024 units) splits into sixteen smaller 8-bit squares (64 units each).

beats.say: Yet when an H one hundred switches from sixteen-bit to eight-bit numbers, its throughput doubles rather than quadrupling: from nine hundred and eighty-nine trillion to nearly two thousand trillion.
beats.show: A throughput meter jumps from 989.4 TFLOP/s at 16-bit to 1,978.9 TFLOP/s at 8-bit: a 2× increase, not 4×.

beats.say: Why twice and not four times? Because of operand delivery. The internal wires carrying numbers to the units have a fixed bit width.
beats.show: Data paths feeding the multipliers highlight with fixed bandwidth capacity: 'delivery paths move fixed bits per tick'.

beats.say: The square law sets how much arithmetic fits in silicon. Data delivery sets how fast it can be fed.
beats.show: A summary card balances the two constraints: 'Silicon area allows 4×; delivery bandwidth limits to 2×'. Takeaway: 'operand delivery paths, not multiplier area, set the throughput scaling'.

scenes.name: the generational format ladder
scenes.visual: A timeline of format introductions: FP16 on Volta (125 TFLOP/s), FP8 on Hopper (1,979 TFLOP/s), and FP4 on Blackwell (9,000 TFLOP/s), showing a compounded 72-fold gain.

beats.say: Every tensor-core generation has introduced a narrower native format.
beats.show: A ladder of format standards appears: 'FP16 (2017)', 'FP8 (2022)', and 'FP4 (2024)'.

beats.say: Volta introduced sixteen-bit tensor cores in twenty-seventeen at a hundred and twenty-five trillion operations a second.
Hopper introduced eight-bit floats at nearly two thousand trillion. Blackwell introduces four-bit floats at nine thousand trillion operations a second.
beats.show: Subsequent milestones light up: 'Hopper H100 · 8-bit FP8 · 1,979 TFLOP/s' → 'Blackwell B200 · 4-bit FP4 · 9,000 TFLOP/s'.

beats.say: From Volta's sixteen-bit rate to Blackwell's four-bit rate is a seventy-two-fold increase in dense arithmetic throughput.
beats.show: A massive growth arrow connects V100 125 T to B200 9,000 T: '72× throughput growth across four generations'. Takeaway pill: 'shrinking precision compounds with architectural gains for massive throughput'.

checks.claim: H100 8-bit peak: 989.429 * 2 = 1,978.86 TFLOP/s, quoted as 'nearly two thousand trillion'
